title: The Rerun of Rome
synopsis: A 2011 essay comparing American structural patterns to late Rome: currency debasement, military overextension, infrastructure decay, and declining civic virtue.

content:
*Originally published March 2011. Re-uploaded January 2026 as referenced in a recent article.*

I've been thinking a great deal lately about pattern recognition. I mean it in the older sense here, though my interest in the machine learning kind bleeds into everything. The human brain evolved to detect patterns because patterns kept us alive - the rustle in the grass that preceded the predator, the change of season that preceded famine. We're prediction machines at the core, and we can't switch it off.

So I find myself unable to ignore certain patterns that have been crystallising over the past several years. Patterns connecting the world I see through my window in 2011 to accounts written nearly two millennia ago about a civilisation that at its height must have seemed as permanent and inevitable as the American project seems today.

I want to be clear at the outset that I'm not making a prophecy. Prophecy belongs to charlatans and the self-deceived. What I'm doing is more modest and I hope more useful: asking whether the structural conditions that preceded Rome's long decline are beginning to appear in the American context, and what that might mean for those of us who'll live through the coming decades.

Start with the financial crisis of 2008, which I suspect future historians will treat as more significant than we currently do. The crisis was dramatic enough. What interests me more is the response.

Rome, in its declining centuries, repeatedly debased its currency to paper over structural problems. The denarius, nearly pure silver under Augustus, held barely five percent silver by the reign of Gallienus. Nobody did this out of malice or stupidity. They did it because the alternative - genuine reform of the underlying economic structure - was politically impossible.

Now watch what the Federal Reserve is doing with quantitative easing. I'm not saying it's wrong and I'm not qualified to make that judgement. I'm saying the pattern rhymes. When a state can't or won't address structural problems directly, it turns to monetary manipulation as a substitute for reform. The can gets kicked down the road, and the road shortens with every kick.

Then there's military overextension. I walked past a news stand yesterday and counted references to ongoing operations in Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen and Libya. Rome at its height maintained legions across three continents, which was sustainable while the empire expanded and the spoils of conquest funded further conquest. It stopped being sustainable when the expansion halted and the commitments didn't.

The United States has over seven hundred military bases in foreign countries. Seven hundred. The annual defence budget exceeds the next dozen nations combined. And we struggle to articulate what victory would look like in any current engagement. We're fighting to maintain rather than to expand, exactly as Rome did in its later centuries, and the psychological shift that represents is profound even though it goes largely unacknowledged.

I'm struck too by the growing distance between the political class and everyone else. The Roman Republic had a concept called virtus - a civic virtue binding citizens to the state and to each other. By the late Empire it had been replaced by something transactional. The state provided bread and circuses, the populace provided acquiescence, and the relationship became one of mutual cynicism rather than mutual obligation.

Consider American politics in 2011. The Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street represent, in their very different ways, a deep loss of faith in institutional legitimacy. People right across the spectrum have begun to suspect the game is rigged and the system serves interests other than their own. That suspicion may be more or less accurate in its specifics, and its existence as a widespread phenomenon is itself the significant fact. Legitimacy, once lost, is extraordinarily difficult to rebuild.

The infrastructure question troubles me as well. Rome built roads and aqueducts that functioned for centuries, and in the period of decline the maintenance was deferred, then neglected, then forgotten. The American Society of Civil Engineers currently grades American infrastructure at D. Not a metaphorical D - an actual letter grade in an actual report. Bridges are structurally deficient. Water systems leak. The electrical grid runs on technology a 1960s engineer would recognise immediately.

There's something almost too neat about a civilisation that can't maintain its bridges. Bridges are such obvious symbols of connection, of a nation bound together, that their decay reads like heavy-handed fiction. And here we are.

I want to address an objection. Someone could argue these comparisons are facile - that America in 2011 is nothing like Rome in 200 or 300 CE, that the technological and social contexts differ so completely as to make the comparison meaningless. The objection has real merit and I think it misses the deeper point.

The specific causes of Roman decline are debated by historians and probably always will be. Lead poisoning, Christianity, barbarian invasions, soil exhaustion, moral decay - the list runs on. Underneath all of them sits a more general pattern. Complex systems, whether empires or ecosystems or economies, absorb shocks and hold their structure up to a point. Past that point they undergo phase transitions and reorganise into different configurations. The old system doesn't so much fall as transform into something its own inhabitants wouldn't recognise as continuous with what came before.

What I'm asking is whether America has begun approaching such a transition. The timing doesn't interest me much and I've no view on whether it arrives in my lifetime. What interests me is whether the early signatures of systemic stress are becoming visible to anyone who cares to look.

I don't think that's cause for despair. Rome's decline was also a transformation. New forms of social organisation emerged from the old, and the medieval world that followed wasn't worse than Rome in any absolute sense, merely different. People went on loving and creating and reaching for meaning throughout.

I do think it's cause for seriousness. If we're in the early stages of a major historical transition, then the choices made over the coming decades will shape what follows. The Romans of the third century couldn't have prevented the transformation of their world. They could have influenced its direction, and some of them did, and their influence reaches us still.

What I'm really arguing for is a quality of attention. Not panic, which is useless, and not denial, which is worse than useless. A clear-eyed willingness to look at the patterns in front of us and ask what they might mean. The rustle in the grass may be nothing at all. It may be something. Either way it seems worth noticing, and noticing is free.
